hook: In 1831, a crew in Virginia cut wheat with hand tools while a horse-drawn machine beside them did the work of many workers. Within a few decades, farms across Britain and North America were growing more food with fewer people, and the people who were no longer needed on farms moved to towns.

prereq.q: Which was a result of the First Agricultural Revolution?
options: People moved to factories in towns
Crops crossed the Atlantic by ship
prereq.why: Farming tied people to their fields, so villages formed.

prereq.q: In stage 2 of the demographic transition model, what happens?
options: Death rates fall while birth rates stay high
Birth rates fall while death rates stay high
Both rates are low and close together
prereq.why: Better food and health lower death rates first, so population grows fast.

ideas: The Second Agricultural Revolution began in Britain and western Europe in the 1700s and spread to North America in the 1800s, alongside the rise of factories.
Its changes: crop rotation (the Norfolk four-field system), selective breeding, enclosure and mechanization (seed drill, steel plow, reaper).
Effects: more food per worker, better diets and lower death rates, and fewer farm jobs, which pushed people to towns and factory work.

misconception.wrong: The Second Agricultural Revolution means farmers began growing crops for the first time.
misconception.right: That was the First Agricultural Revolution. The second changed how existing farms worked: rotation, breeding, enclosure and machines, from the 1700s.

summary: The Second Agricultural Revolution, from the 1700s in Britain and the 1800s in North America, brought crop rotation, selective breeding, enclosure and mechanization. Each farm worker grew more food, diets and life spans improved, and people no longer needed on farms moved to towns.
